dropped.text: The Global Positioning System is owned by the United States Space Force and operated by Mission Delta 31.
The orbits are arranged so that at least 6 satellites are always within line of sight from everywhere on the Earth.
Each satellite acts like a floating radio station that carries an accurate record of its own position and time.
Each satellite carries very stable atomic clocks that are synchronized with reference clocks on the ground.
An atomic clock measures time by monitoring the resonant frequency of atoms.
Since the speed of radio waves is constant and independent of the satellite speed, time delay relates directly to distance.
Your receiver compares the bit sequence received from the satellite with an internally generated version.
Trilateration is the use of distances for determining the unknown position coordinates of a point of interest.
While the satellites carry ultra-precise atomic clocks, your smartphone relies on a cheap internal quartz crystal clock.

dropped.text: At a minimum, four satellites must be in view for the receiver to compute three position coordinates and its clock deviation.
According to special relativity, the faster an object moves, the slower its time appears to pass.
The atomic clocks moving at orbital speeds tick more slowly than stationary clocks by a fraction of 8.349 parts in 10 to the 11th.
